e-01.title: Combine two lines of the library notice to check Ben's plan
e-01.goal: Combine two different lines of the notice (the usual schedule and this week's exception), decide day by day whether your friend's plan works, and tell him in English.
e-01.material:
The notice on the school library door (written in words only, no picture):

Library
Open: Mon, Wed, Fri  3:00-4:00
This week: closed on Friday (cleaning day).

Your friend Ben said, "Let's go to the library on Thursday and on Friday this week!"
e-01.thinking.0: Combine several lines of a notice to make a decision
e-01.thinking.1: Find separate evidence for each day
e-01.thinking.2: Check a friend's plan against the evidence
e-01.s.s1.prompt: Can Ben use the library on both Thursday and Friday this week, as he plans?
e-01.s.s1.hint.0: Look at Thursday and Friday separately, and compare what each line of the notice says about that day.
e-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the 'Open' line and the 'This week' line do different jobs.
e-01.s.s1.r.a: You may not have read both lines of the notice. Check whether Thursday is among the open days, and whether there is a special note about Friday.
e-01.s.s1.r.c: Friday is usually open, but the 'This week' line says something different about this week.
e-01.s.s1.r.d: Look again for whether Thursday is in the list of open days (Open).
e-01.s.s1.explain: Thursday is not one of the open days (Mon, Wed, Fri), and although Friday is usually open, this week it is 'closed on Friday'. So neither day works.
e-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the lines you need to judge Ben's plan (Thursday and Friday).
e-01.s.s2.hint.0: Try removing each line and see whether it becomes harder to judge Thursday or Friday.
e-01.s.s2.hint.1: Keep Ben's words and the lines of the notice separate.
e-01.s.s2.r.a: This is used to judge Thursday, but this line alone does not tell you about this week's Friday (it is usually open). Check whether you need another line too.
e-01.s.s2.r.b: You need this to judge Friday, but this line says nothing about Thursday. Find which line lets you judge Thursday.
e-01.s.s2.r.c: It is only a title, so it has no information about days.
e-01.s.s2.r.d: This sentence is Ben's suggestion. A suggestion is something to check, not evidence.
e-01.s.s2.explain: The Open line shows that Thursday is not an open day, and the This week line shows that Friday is closed this week. Either one alone cannot judge both days. If you chose only one, check which day is left over.
e-01.s.s3.prompt: Reply to Ben in English in one or two sentences. Give the reason you can't go on Thursday and the reason you can't go on Friday.
e-01.s.s3.hint.0: First, write one sentence telling Ben 'no, we can't.'
e-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write one sentence for the Thursday reason and one for the Friday reason, each connected to a line of the notice.
e-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give a reason for Thursday and a reason for Friday?
e-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can you say which line of the notice each of your reasons comes from?
e-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you suggested another day, did you check that it is really an open day? (optional)

e-02.title: Find the confusing sentence in an invitation message
e-02.goal: Find two sentences in a short invitation message that don't match, and rewrite them so friends won't be confused.
e-02.material: This is a message Jun sent to his classmates. (It is written in words only. Each line has a number.)
e-02.thinking.0: Find information that contradicts itself between sentences
e-02.prereq.1: Easy verbs like come / start the game
e-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one sentence that could confuse friends. It is a line that doesn't match another sentence.
e-02.s.s1.hint.0: Collect only the lines that contain numbers (times).
e-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the 'arrival time' and the 'start time'. Which comes first?
e-02.s.s1.explain: It tells people to come at 10, but says the game starts at 9:30. You may change either line 3 or line 4. Line 1 (the park on Sunday) and line 2 (the park's location) do not conflict with any other line. If you compare the lines with numbers (times), you can see the conflict.
e-02.s.s2.prompt: What could happen if this message were sent as it is?
e-02.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine a friend who receives the message looks at the clock and does exactly what it says.
e-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare: had the game already started by the time that friend arrived?
e-02.s.s2.o.a: A friend who comes at 10 misses a game that has already started.
e-02.s.s2.o.b: A friend who comes at 9:30 waits in an empty park before the game starts.
e-02.s.s2.r.b: This can really happen to a friend who believes the 9:30 start and arrives then. But the most direct problem caused by the conflict with 'come at 10' is a.
e-02.s.s2.o.c: Friends end up coming on Saturday instead of Sunday.
e-02.s.s2.r.c: The day is clearly Sunday. The problem is the time.
e-02.s.s2.explain: The problem depends on which of the two times you follow. If you follow 10, you miss the game (a); if you follow 9:30, you are confused because it differs from what the other line says (b). Either way, it happens because the two times don't match.
e-02.s.s2.acc.0: A friend who believes the 9:30 start and arrives then to wait is also a real result of the conflict. a is for a friend who followed '10', and b is for a friend who followed '9:30'.
e-02.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the two sentences (arrival time and game start time) in English so that the times match.
e-02.s.s3.hint.0: You can change just one of the two times. Decide first which one to change.
e-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put the arrival time before the start time, and write both times as numbers side by side to compare them.
e-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Of the two times you wrote, which is earlier? Does the arrival time come first?
e-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you picture how a friend would act after reading this message?
e-02.s.s3.modelNote.0: I made the arrival time earlier.
e-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: I made the start time later.

e-03.title: Decide what to ask before replying
e-03.goal: Decide what information you really need before replying to an invitation text, and write a short English reply that asks for it.
e-03.material:
You got a text from your friend Ari. "Let's play soccer tomorrow!"
You think it sounds good, but this text alone isn't enough to decide whether you can go.
e-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
e-03.thinking.2: Write a reply that includes questions
e-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you must know in order to answer 'I can go.'
e-03.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the answer to each question can already be found in the text.
e-03.s.s1.hint.1: Try each question one by one: if you don't have its answer, could you say 'I'll come'?
e-03.s.s1.r.a: Time is needed. But with only this, you don't know where to go. Check whether anything else is needed.
e-03.s.s1.r.b: Place is needed. But with only this, you don't know what time it is. Check whether anything else is needed.
e-03.s.s1.r.c: A ball is nice to have, but it isn't needed to decide whether you can go.
e-03.s.s1.r.d: It might help, but you can decide whether you can go without it. Think about whether it is really necessary information.
e-03.s.s1.r.e: Ari already said let's play soccer. This asks about something you already know.
e-03.s.s1.r.f: Knowing the reason is good for curiosity, but it isn't needed to decide whether you can go. A question isn't necessary just because it starts with a question word.
e-03.s.s1.explain: If you don't know the time and place, you can't decide whether it fits your schedule or whether you can get there. If you chose only one, test again: without the other one, could you say 'I'll come'? (If you know only the time, you don't know where to go; if you know only the place, you don't know what time.)
e-03.s.s1.acc.0: It is natural to want to know who is coming too. But the most important point is that you can't answer without the time and place.
e-03.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to Ari in English. Show that you want to join, and include a question asking for the information you chose above.
e-03.s.s2.hint.0: First, write a short phrase that means 'Sounds good!'
e-03.s.s2.hint.1: You can also join the two questions you chose into one sentence.
e-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: After reading my reply, can Ari tell me the time and place?
e-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does it include both a friendly response and the questions?
e-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: I asked using a longer sentence.

e-04.title: What does Jun want? Revise your thinking as clues are added
e-04.goal: Each time a clue in the conversation is added, guess again what the speaker wants, and explain how your guess changed.
e-04.material: At home, Jun is talking to his mom. His words will be shown one piece at a time.
e-04.thinking.0: Guess the hidden meaning of words
e-04.thinking.1: Revise a judgment based on new information
e-04.prereq.0: Easy words like small, hurt, closed
e-04.s.s1.prompt: Read Jun's words one piece at a time, and each time guess what Jun wants.
e-04.s.s1.hint.0: Find one new word in this piece.
e-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether your earlier guess fits the new clue.
e-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable guess about what Jun wants from his mom, from this sentence alone?
e-04.s.s1.st.0.after: You can't know exactly from one sentence. He might want new shoes, or he might just be stating a fact.
e-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: He wants to skip P.E. class.
e-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: There is nothing yet in the clues about P.E. class or skipping.
e-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: He hopes his mom will buy him new shoes.
e-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: He might just be saying that his shoes are small.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Jun: "They hurt when I run. We have P.E. (physical education) class tomorrow."
e-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Read the new clue and guess again what Jun wants.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 'It hurts' and 'P.E. tomorrow' together make it clear he wants it solved by tomorrow. If you thought in the first step that he was 'just stating a fact', you need to revise your guess here.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: He wants to fix it so his feet don't hurt before P.E. class tomorrow.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Again, he is just stating a fact.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Saying his feet hurt and he has P.E. tomorrow is a clue that he wants it solved. That was possible in the first step, but now it doesn't fit the clues.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: He wants to skip P.E. class.
e-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: He never said he wants to skip. Reading it as looking for a solution from 'it hurts' and 'P.E. tomorrow' is closer to the clues.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Read the last clue and guess what Jun will do.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The store is closed today, so 'new shoes today' is blocked. Plans like going to another store or talking about a friend's shoes both fit the new clue. If you only thought of new shoes, you need to change your plan from buying them today.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: He goes to the store today and buys new shoes.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It doesn't fit the clue that the store is closed today.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: He asks his mom to go to another store early tomorrow morning.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is also a possible plan. But the idea Jun actually brings up at the end is about a friend.
e-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: He thinks about borrowing shoes from a friend with the same foot size.
e-04.s.s1.reflect: Did your guess change at each step? If it did, name one sentence that was the reason.
e-04.s.s2.prompt: Which clue makes Jun's wish read as changing from 'just saying' to 'solving it by tomorrow'?
e-04.s.s2.hint.0: Read the three clues in order and find where the number of possible guesses first got smaller.
e-04.s.s2.hint.1: Read with each clue removed and test whether the meaning 'he wants to fix it' still remains.
e-04.s.s2.r.b: This sentence was there from the start, and by itself it allowed several guesses.
e-04.s.s2.r.c: This clue blocked one way to solve it (the store), but the wish to solve it was already shown by the earlier clues.
e-04.s.s2.explain: 'It hurts' and 'P.E. tomorrow' create a problem with a time limit, so Jun reads as wanting it solved.

e-05.title: Telling different people about the same situation
e-05.goal: Write in English about the same situation (missing the club because of a dentist appointment) to a teacher and to a friend, each with a fitting tone and length.
e-05.material: There is an English club today at 3:30, but you have a dentist appointment at the same time, so you can't go. You need to tell the club teacher, Ms. Han, with a message, and a friend in the same club with a short text.
e-05.thinking.0: Compare and choose expressions according to the person and situation
e-05.thinking.1: Write to meet the conditions of politeness and length
e-05.prereq.0: Polite expressions like could / would / please
e-05.prereq.1: The expression I have a ... appointment
e-05.s.s1.prompt: Which is the best message to send to Ms. Han? (You will write to your friend in the next step.)
e-05.s.s1.hint.0: Look for an apology or a request in each message.
e-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare them by imagining how the teacher would feel when receiving each message.
e-05.s.s1.r.b: The reason and situation are clear, but with no apology or request it can feel like you are just announcing it to the teacher.
e-05.s.s1.r.c: It gives a reason but sounds like pushing the blame away, which could upset the other person.
e-05.s.s1.r.d: The tone is friendly but still polite. The grammar is fine too.
e-05.s.s1.explain: a and d have an apology, a reason, and a request. a is more formal and d is lighter, but both are polite. b is clear and respectful, but without an apology or request it can read as less polite. In c, the tone of pushing blame away may make the other person uncomfortable. The level of formality expected differs by school and by teacher.
e-05.s.s1.acc.0: If you are close to the teacher, a friendly and polite tone like d also fits. a is a more formal expression.
e-05.s.s1.acc.1: b has a clear reason and situation and a polite title (Ms. Han), so it is fine as a short notice. But with no apology or request, it can read as less polite than a and d.
e-05.s.s2.prompt: Write the message to Ms. Han yourself. Say that you can't come and the reason (dentist appointment), and include a polite expression (an apology or a request).
e-05.s.s2.hint.0: First think of what you would add if you were speaking to your teacher in Korean, then find how to say that meaning in English.
e-05.s.s2.hint.1: Try writing in this order: the sentence about not coming, the reason sentence, the request sentence.
e-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the tone one that won't upset the teacher when she reads it? Which word does that job?
e-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the reason understood right away?
e-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: If you added something you want (such as getting the materials), does it sound like a request?
e-05.s.s3.prompt: This time it is a text to a friend in the same club. Write the same situation briefly in 18 words or fewer, in a casual tone. (Do not use formal expressions like Dear or I'm afraid.)
e-05.s.s3.hint.0: Keep only the information you must keep from your message to the teacher (the reason, and that you can't come).
e-05.s.s3.hint.1: Use contractions (can't) or short words, and count the words.
e-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Compared with what you wrote to the teacher, which words disappeared and which stayed?
e-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Even though it is short, can your friend tell the reason?
e-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: A friendly tone with an apology and a question.

e-06.title: Find the sentences with overlapping schedules in a group message
e-06.goal: Find two schedule sentences in a group message that don't match, explain what confusion they could cause, and rewrite them.
e-06.material: This is a message that the leader of a science group project posted in the group chat. (Each line has a number. Afternoon times are written as p.m.)
e-06.thinking.1: Predict the problem that will happen
e-06.prereq.0: by / before / after + day or time
e-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose one sentence that could cause a problem for group members following the schedule. It is the line whose time order doesn't match another sentence.
e-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find all the lines that have times, and put the times in time order.
e-06.s.s1.hint.1: Which comes first: the deadline for sending or the time for putting together?
e-06.s.s1.explain: The putting-together time is Thursday 4:30 p.m., but the parts deadline is Thursday 9:00 p.m. The deadline is later than the putting-together time, so the two lines (line 2 and line 3) conflict. Lines 1 and 4 are about the Friday deadline and printing, so they don't conflict with each other.
e-06.s.s2.prompt: What would really happen if people followed this message as it is?
e-06.s.s2.hint.0: Suppose a group member sends their part exactly on 'Thursday night'.
e-06.s.s2.hint.1: What has the leader already finished by that point?
e-06.s.s2.o.a: A part due by 9 might not have arrived yet when the parts are put together at 4:30.
e-06.s.s2.o.b: All the parts arrive before the putting-together work, so the poster is finished early.
e-06.s.s2.r.b: The putting-together work is at 4:30 p.m., and parts are accepted until 9:00 p.m. Compare the times again.
e-06.s.s2.o.c: There is no time left to print before class on Friday.
e-06.s.s2.r.c: The problem is the order within Thursday. There is still time until Friday morning.
e-06.s.s2.explain: The putting-together comes first, yet parts are accepted until later than that, so a part sent late may be left out.
e-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite one of the conflicting lines (or both) in English. Make the times and days match each other.
e-06.s.s3.hint.0: First decide which of the two lines' times to change.
e-06.s.s3.hint.1: After changing it, read again to check that the order 'parts deadline → putting together → printing' is right by the times.
e-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Please send me your part by ...
e-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the deadline for receiving parts come before the putting-together time? Compare the two times as numbers.
e-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there still time before the Friday morning deadline?
e-06.s.s3.modelNote.0: I moved the parts deadline earlier.
e-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: I moved the putting-together time later and added a reason.

e-07.title: Combine two notices to work out the bus departure time
e-07.goal: Combine two notices posted on different dates (the original time and a later change) to work out the new departure time, and correct a friend's misunderstanding using evidence.
e-07.material:
Two notices are posted on the bulletin board at the bus stop. (Written in words only.)

Notice A (posted on Monday): "Bus 5 leaves at 7:40 a.m."
Notice B (posted on Wednesday): "From Thursday, Bus 5 will leave 10 minutes earlier. Please be at the stop on time."

Your friend Hana: "Bus 5 leaves at 7:50 on Thursday."
Your friend Jae: "Then on Friday it leaves at the same time as on Thursday."
e-07.thinking.0: Combine several pieces of information to reach a conclusion
e-07.thinking.1: Understand how a later notice changes an earlier one
e-07.prereq.0: Expressions like earlier / later / from + day
e-07.prereq.1: Reading times and calculating with time
e-07.s.s1.prompt: Judging from the two notices, is Hana right?
e-07.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the dates when the two notices were posted. Which one is later?
e-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether earlier means 'sooner' or 'later', and calculate from 7:40.
e-07.s.s1.o.a: She's right. Adding B's 10 minutes to A's 7:40 gives 7:50.
e-07.s.s1.r.a: You may have read earlier as if it were 'later'. Check the meaning of earlier again.
e-07.s.s1.o.b: She's wrong. B says it leaves 10 minutes earlier, so it is 7:30.
e-07.s.s1.o.c: We can't tell. We can't decide which of the two notices is correct.
e-07.s.s1.r.c: The two notices do not contradict each other. B is a later notice that changes A's time.
e-07.s.s1.explain: Notice B was posted later and says 10 minutes earlier than A's time. 10 minutes before 7:40 is 7:30.
e-07.s.s2.prompt: Jae said, "On Friday it's the same time as Thursday." How can you judge this statement from the notices?
e-07.s.s2.hint.0: Try swapping 'on Thursday' and 'from Thursday' and compare whether the meaning changes.
e-07.s.s2.hint.1: Look for words in the notice that tell you when it ends.
e-07.s.s2.o.a: 'From Thursday' means continuing from Thursday on, so Friday is the same as Thursday.
e-07.s.s2.o.b: 'From Thursday' means only Thursday changes for that one day.
e-07.s.s2.r.b: 'From Thursday' and 'on Thursday' are different. 'From' points to a starting point.
e-07.s.s2.o.c: Friday isn't directly in the notice, so it seems you need to check.
e-07.s.s2.r.c: Being careful is reasonable. But the expression 'From Thursday' already includes the days after it.
e-07.s.s2.explain: 'From Thursday' means the new time applies starting on Thursday. If there is no word telling when it ends, Friday is the same. Thinking of asking the staff because it isn't written directly is also reasonable.
e-07.s.s2.acc.0: Wanting to ask the staff because Friday isn't written directly in the notice is also reasonable. But 'From Thursday' usually means it continues afterward.
e-07.s.s3.prompt: Reply to Hana in English. Say what time the bus leaves on Thursday, and give a reason based on the notices.
e-07.s.s3.hint.0: Start from Notice A's time, and write what Notice B says it changes.
e-07.s.s3.hint.1: Add one sentence on 'why 7:50 is wrong.'
e-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I think it leaves at ... because ...
e-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear which of the two notices your evidence comes from?
e-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why 7:50 is wrong?
e-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: A short answer that argues from the meaning of a word.

e-08.title: Write a club notice that isn't confusing
e-08.goal: Point out why an ambiguous notice is confusing, and rewrite the same content in English so anyone who reads it understands without a mistake.
e-08.material:
This is a notice posted on the bulletin board.

"Art Club meeting this Friday or next week at 3 or 4 in room 2 or the gym. Bring something."

Friends who read this notice went to different places and couldn't meet.
e-08.thinking.1: Make a notice that removes ambiguity
e-08.prereq.0: Expressions for day, time, and place
e-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything friends were confused about.
e-08.s.s1.hint.0: Mark the parts of the notice that contain 'or', and the parts with vague words whose meaning you can't tell (such as something).
e-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check part by part whether a reader can believe just one thing and act on it.
e-08.s.s1.r.a: It is true that the date is ambiguous. Check whether the other items let the reader act on just one thing too.
e-08.s.s1.r.b: It is true that the time is ambiguous. Check whether the other items let the reader act on just one thing too.
e-08.s.s1.r.c: It is true that the place is ambiguous. Check whether the other items let the reader act on just one thing too.
e-08.s.s1.r.d: It is true that what to bring is ambiguous. Check whether the other items let the reader act on just one thing too.
e-08.s.s1.r.e: It is clear whose meeting it is. Choose only the parts a reader could understand in two or more ways.
e-08.s.s1.explain: The date, time, and place are all ambiguous because of 'or', and what to bring is ambiguous because you can't tell what 'something' is. If you chose only some, test again whether a reader can act on just one thing for the items you left out.
e-08.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the notice for the same meeting in English without any misunderstanding. Decide and write the day, time, place, and what to bring.
e-08.s.s2.hint.0: In your head, make a table where you fix one thing each for day, time, place, and what to bring.
e-08.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine whether a friend who has never been to the meeting could find it using only this notice.
e-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your notice have any part where you put two options with 'or'? (For example, two times or two places)
e-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Even for a friend seeing it for the first time, can they tell where to go?
e-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Are both the date (day) and the time set to one thing?
e-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: A friendly tone. The 'or' for what to bring is just a choice, not ambiguous.

e-09.title: Before answering a junior's 'Could you look at it at some point?'
e-09.goal: Pick out the missing information in a vague request, and write an English reply that politely includes the questions you need.
e-09.material:
You got a message from a student one year below you. You barely know each other.

"Hi! Sorry to bother you, but could you look at my essay at some point? Thanks!!"

You want to help, but you are busy this week.
e-09.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
e-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you need to know before replying, so you can decide whether you can help and help properly.
e-09.s.s1.hint.0: Underline the vague words in the message, and write one line for each on why that word makes your decision hard.
e-09.s.s1.hint.1: Try each question one by one: if it has no answer, could you say 'Yes, I'll do it'?
e-09.s.s1.r.a: The deadline is needed. But from this alone you don't know what kind of help is needed. Check whether there is another question you need.
e-09.s.s1.r.b: The kind of help is needed. But from this alone you don't know by when it has to be done. Check whether there is another question you need.
e-09.s.s1.r.c: The length is needed to estimate the time. Check whether other questions are needed too.
e-09.s.s1.r.d: Last year's grades are not directly related to whether you can help with this essay, or how.
e-09.s.s1.r.e: Whether they have other help doesn't change whether you can help, or how.
e-09.s.s1.explain: 'At some point' is vague about when, and 'look at' is vague about the kind of help. You need to know the deadline, the help wanted, and the length to decide whether you can make time. If you chose only some, test whether you could help without the answer to a question you left out.
e-09.s.s1.acc.0: The deadline and the kind of help wanted are the key points, and the length is something you learn after receiving it, so leaving it out is reasonable.
e-09.s.s1.acc.1: It is also reasonable to first decide with the deadline and length whether you can make time, and ask about the kind of help later.
e-09.s.s1.acc.2: Even though you are busy this week, you can first estimate whether you can help from the kind of help needed and the length. But you will need to know the deadline soon.
e-09.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to the junior in English. Politely show that you are willing to help, and include at least two of the questions you chose above.
e-09.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on two questions that would change whether you can help, or how.
e-09.s.s2.hint.1: Write one question per sentence, and put a phrase about helping at the very start.
e-09.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Sure, I'd be happy to help! ...
e-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: After reading my reply, can the junior tell me the deadline and the help they want?
e-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you see both the wish to help and the questions?
e-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the tone right for someone you barely know?
e-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: A more polite and specific format.

e-10.title: A polite refusal, or is there still a chance?
e-10.goal: As each sentence of a polite email is revealed, revise your judgment about the other person's real intention, and write a fitting reply.
e-10.material: You sent a proposal for making a school vegetable garden to Ms. Rowe, who is in charge at school. The reply email opens one sentence at a time.
e-10.thinking.0: Infer the intention behind a polite tone
e-10.thinking.1: Revise a judgment with new information
e-10.thinking.2: Write a reply that fits the situation
e-10.prereq.1: Basic understanding of polite refusal expressions
e-10.s.s1.prompt: Read the email one piece at a time, and each time choose your judgment of whether the proposal will be accepted.
e-10.s.s1.hint.0: First decide whether the new sentence changes the meaning of the earlier one or continues it.
e-10.s.s1.hint.1: Mark the words that change the flow (But) and the specific words like dates and purposes.
e-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable judgment from this sentence alone?
e-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Praise alone doesn't show the decision. It could be the opening of a gentle refusal, or just a greeting. The next sentence matters.
e-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It will likely be approved, and she will let us know soon.
e-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 'Interesting' is praise, but it is not a word of decision or approval.
e-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: She may intend to refuse politely.
e-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can't know the decision yet, and need to see the next sentence.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.after: The range expression 'this year' matters. If you read it as a 'polite refusal' in the first step, this sentence supports that reading, but it is not a permanent refusal yet.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It says this year is difficult, and says nothing yet about afterward.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It means a complete refusal from now on, regardless of this year.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It only said 'this year's budget.' It never said a permanent refusal.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is only a budget problem, so it will be solved soon and we can start this year.
e-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It said the budget has already been set.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: Read to the last sentence and judge again.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.after: The flow changes with 'But', and the deadline (Friday), the purpose (director), and the time (March) are specific. Whether you read it as not yet decided or as an intention to move ahead, if you had firmly decided on 'polite refusal' earlier, you need to revise your judgment.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is just a courtesy, so there is no need to reply.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Someone who only wants to refuse doesn't give a deadline (Friday) and a purpose (director, March) in detail.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: She hasn't decided whether to refuse yet, and is gathering information to judge.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is also a possible reading. But 'I will show it to the director before the March budget meeting' is closer to wanting to move forward.
e-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: She is interested, and is asking for materials so it can be pushed forward at the March budget meeting.
e-10.s.s1.reflect: Tell how your judgment changed in the third step after you judged 'difficult' in the second step. Which words (But, by Friday, before ... March) were the reason?
e-10.s.s2.prompt: Write how your judgment in the first step differed from your judgment in the last (third) step, and which expressions made it different. You may write in Korean or English. (If it didn't change, write why it stayed the same.)
e-10.s.s2.hint.0: First, write in one sentence the choice you made in step 1.
e-10.s.s2.hint.1: Among the expressions that newly appeared in step 3 (But, Friday, March, etc.), choose one that changed your judgment.
e-10.s.s2.placeholder: Example: At first I thought ... but because of ...
e-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write the judgment you first chose?
e-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you pick out and write which expression from the email changed your judgment?
e-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: If it didn't change, did you explain why using clues from the email?
e-10.s.s2.model.0: At first I thought it was a polite refusal, but in the last sentence I saw that after 'But' she asked for an estimate by Friday, so I changed to thinking she is interested.
e-10.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to Ms. Rowe in English. Show thanks and understanding of the situation, and promise to send what was requested by the requested day (Friday).
e-10.s.s3.hint.0: Reread what is requested in the last sentence of the email (what, and by when) and carry it over into your answer as it is.
e-10.s.s3.hint.1: Try writing in this order: one sentence of thanks, one sentence of understanding, one sentence of promise.
e-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Thank you for your reply. ...
e-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did your reply respond exactly to Ms. Rowe's last request?
e-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there an expression showing you understand that this year's budget doesn't allow it?
e-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid showing too much disappointment?
e-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that proposes adjusting the plan.

e-11.title: Examining the claim 'Scores dropped, so it's the Wi-Fi's fault'
e-11.goal: Evaluate whether the cause-and-effect reasoning in a school newspaper letter is sufficient, decide what information is needed to check the claim, and politely write a counterargument to the author in English.
e-11.material:
A reader's letter in the school newspaper (an imaginary text):

"Last year, our school's average English score was 78. This year, after the school started free Wi-Fi, it fell to 72. So the Wi-Fi caused the drop. Therefore we should turn the Wi-Fi off."
e-11.thinking.0: Find the leaps in an argument
e-11.thinking.1: Choose the information needed for checking
e-11.prereq.0: Cause-and-effect expressions like therefore / so / caused
e-11.prereq.1: Disagreeing politely (I see your point, however ...)
e-11.s.s1.prompt: Choose one sentence in this text that speaks as if it were certain fact even though the evidence is lacking.
e-11.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into 'something that happened' or 'a claim about a cause or what should be done.'
e-11.s.s1.hint.1: Test whether the claim lines follow from the fact lines before them alone.
e-11.s.s1.explain: Line 3 ('So the Wi-Fi caused the drop.') jumps from 'it happened afterward' to 'it is the cause.' The 'we should turn it off' in line 4 also lacks evidence, but it leans on the leap in line 3. Lines 1 and 2 are statements of fact about the scores and the time.
e-11.s.s2.prompt: What information would help you check 'The Wi-Fi is the cause of the score drop'? Choose all that apply.
e-11.s.s2.hint.0: Think of two reasons other than the Wi-Fi why scores could change.
e-11.s.s2.hint.1: Judge whether each choice could help sort out whether the Wi-Fi or another reason is the cause.
e-11.s.s2.o.a: How English scores changed in the same year at another school without Wi-Fi
e-11.s.s2.r.a: Comparison is a good method. Also look at whether you can check differences in test difficulty or in the group of students.
e-11.s.s2.o.b: Whether this year's English test was harder than last year's
e-11.s.s2.r.b: If the test changed, it is an important reason. Also look at comparing with other schools and at the student group.
e-11.s.s2.o.c: How many students like English class
e-11.s.s2.r.c: How much students like class may be related to scores, but it cannot sort out whether the Wi-Fi is the cause.
e-11.s.s2.o.d: How much the Wi-Fi installation cost
e-11.s.s2.r.d: The cost is related to the decision to install it, but has nothing to do with why scores dropped.
e-11.s.s2.o.e: Whether students actually used their phones during English class
e-11.s.s2.r.e: This is information that checks the path. Also look at other reasons (the test, the student group, other schools).
e-11.s.s2.o.f: Whether this year's students are a different group from last year's students (skills, amount of study, etc.)
e-11.s.s2.explain: Comparing with other schools (a), checking test difficulty (b), and checking whether it was actually used during class (e) and differences in the student group (f) lets you sort out whether Wi-Fi or another reason is the cause. The number of students who like class and the installation cost are not directly related to the cause.
e-11.s.s2.acc.0: Comparing with other schools and checking the test difficulty alone are already enough to help sort out other reasons.
e-11.s.s2.acc.1: If you also check whether it was actually used during class, you can see the path through which the Wi-Fi may have worked.
e-11.s.s2.acc.2: Differences in the student group are also a common other reason for a change in scores.
e-11.s.s3.prompt: Write a 2-3 sentence counterargument to the writer in English. Accept the fact that scores dropped, but explain that the claim that the Wi-Fi is the cause is not yet sufficient, and give one way to check it or one other reason.
e-11.s.s3.hint.0: First, in one sentence, acknowledge the part the writer got right (scores dropped).
e-11.s.s3.hint.1: Then write one specific reason why it is not enough to call it 'the cause' (which other reason or comparison).
e-11.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I see your point, but ...
e-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did your writing accept the fact that scores dropped?
e-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give one reason why it is not enough to state firmly that it is 'the cause'?
e-11.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the tone one that points out the logic without attacking the writer?

e-12.title: When 'It's fine.' isn't fine: creating a dialogue
e-12.goal: Judge that words like 'It's fine.' may not mean what they literally say, and create a short English dialogue about that kind of situation to meet the conditions.
e-12.material: A says to B, "I'm sorry I forgot to call you last night." B can answer this in several ways. (Written in words only.)
e-12.thinking.0: Infer hidden intention from tone and context
e-12.thinking.1: Create a dialogue that meets the conditions
e-12.prereq.1: Expressions like Are you sure? / You sound ...
e-12.s.s1.prompt: Of B's answers, which one is most likely to be pretending to be fine when actually not fine?
e-12.s.s1.hint.0: Read each answer aloud, and imagine whether someone who was really fine would say it that way.
e-12.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether each answer includes a 'reason it's fine' or 'something wanted', or whether those are missing.
e-12.s.s1.r.a: It speaks casually while giving a reason. The reason for being fine is in the sentence.
e-12.s.s1.r.c: It may be awkward because it is said too strongly, but it is hard to judge the feeling from the sentence alone.
e-12.s.s1.r.d: It says it's fine, but also states what it wants. It hides less.
e-12.s.s1.explain: If someone says only a short, flat 'It's fine.', neither a reason nor a feeling shows, so it is easily read as hiding the inner feeling. But you can't be sure from the sentence alone, and you have to look at tone and context together.
e-12.s.s1.acc.0: An overly emphasized 'totally' can actually be a sign of covering up not being fine.
e-12.s.s1.acc.1: Hesitating at 'Just...' is a sign that the person is not completely fine. But it is less likely, since the person is telling part of how they feel.
e-12.s.s2.prompt:
Create an English dialogue that meets the conditions below. Start each line with A: or B:, and write at least 4 lines.
Condition 1) B says it's fine with words like 'fine' or 'okay', but actually seems upset.
Condition 2) A notices this and asks gently (use a question mark).
Condition 3) At the end, B says a little of how they really feel.
e-12.s.s2.hint.0: First choose one situation (forgot a promise, a gift, a test result, etc.).
e-12.s.s2.hint.1: Make B's first answer short, and start A's question briefly, like 'Are you sure?'
e-12.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you feel in the dialogue that B's words ('fine') and B's real feeling are different? In which line?
e-12.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is A's question gentle, not blaming?
e-12.s.s2.selfAssess.2: In the last line, did B say a little of how they really feel?
e-12.s.s2.modelNote.0: A flow where the real feeling shows in an apology situation.
e-12.s.s2.modelNote.1: A dialogue that meets the same conditions with a different situation.
